s06.slug: TUESDAY · 7:15 AM · DELGADO HALL, 412 — THE NEWS FEED
body: The window in 412 faces the ridge, and at a quarter past seven on Candlemas the ridge still has the sun, so the only light in the room is the MacBook’s, laid up under Theo’s chin. He is standing at his desk in the wine-colored robe with a mug of tea going cold in one hand, reading, and he has not woken Jack to do it. The retired egg keeps vigil in its cup on the nightstand. On the other desk the envelope for Trumbull leans against the lamp, waiting for a mailbox.
The bedsprings give Jack away. “Costigan,” Theo says, without turning. “Sit up. You’re being remembered in the prayers of the faithful.”
He clears his throat, and the voice comes down over him like a stole: the lector at the twelve-ten, slow, a little through the nose, every name given its full weight.

body.name: Tommy Hritz
body.text: COSTIGAN WTF  youtube.com — SWEETWATER GIRL SINGING BIRTHDAY SEX IN SB!!!
body.meta: Yesterday at 9:10pm · 41 people like this · 23 comments

body: “For Thomas Hritz, of Youngstown, Ohio,” Theo reads, “who has discovered capital letters and does not intend to give them back.” Jack, sitting up, gives him nothing. “Lord, hear our prayer,” Theo answers for him, and scrolls.

“For Douglas Pruitt, who was awake at twelve fifty-one and is presumably still a druid.” A chair rolls back on the far side of the cinderblock, and Doug’s voice comes through it, long and glad and nearly all vowel: “DUUUUUDE.” “Lord,” says Theo, “hear our prayer.”
“For Priya Raman, who has posted the quiet hours to a medium that has none.” He scrolls. “Lord, hear our prayer.”

He goes back to Tommy’s post and clicks through, turns the speaker down to a murmur, and steps aside so Jack can see. Thirty-eight seconds, shot through a windshield from the next lane at a red light, the picture jumping, a girl laughing somewhere behind the phone. It swings, steadies, and there is a face Jack has only ever seen from the inside, mouth open at the top of its lungs and aimed at a girl in sunglasses, who is aiming right back. The hook comes thin and tinny out of the speaker. What Jack hears is her under it, half a beat early and dead certain. He has never caught himself in a mirror making that face.

“Eleven thousand,” Theo says, in his own voice. “Before seven.” He lets the video run on into its sidebar of other people’s cats. “It isn’t the eleven thousand that worries me, Costigan. It’s that each of them has a mother, a pastor, and a cousin in Youngstown.”
“Youngstown’s a big town.”

“Youngstown is a prayer chain with a zip code.” He drags the picture back three seconds and lets it play again, mute. “Now watch her. Photographed professionally since before either of us could shave, and she is the only person in this frame who knows where the camera is, and she doesn’t look at it. I have seen that woman take a forkful of salad at a better angle than most people get married.”
Jack has seen her check the angle on a taco. On the screen she sings at him, and the lens is somebody else’s problem.

“Antiphonal,” Theo reads, and the voice is gone; it simply isn’t there. “Two choirs across an aisle, each answering the other. She took the verse and you took the hook.” He looks at the screen. “Margot is right, which I find upsetting before breakfast.”

He scrolls to the next one, a name from Newman, and his mouth opens for the voice and the voice doesn’t come. He reads the rest to himself. The lid of the MacBook goes down to a crack of light, and his finger stays on it.
“You look happy,” Theo says.
“I am.”
“So the footage suggests.” He takes the towel off its hook and the caddy off the doorknob. “I’m going to stand under hot water until I’m a better man. Expect me at noon.”
The RAZR has been collecting on Jack’s desk since before dawn.

body: He can see the third one entire: the laptop on the oilcloth beside the Folgers can, Nonna in her housedress at the kitchen table, both hands coming together for a girl in a car. The last two came in from Ursuline, where a phone in homeroom is a detention, and Gina has weighed the price and paid it. He reads the last one twice. On the day Danny turns twenty-three, the news from Jack Costigan is that he sang in a car.
It rings in his hand before he can answer a single one. The outside screen says ST BRIGID SCH.
“Happy Candlemas,” Ma says. She has the office voice on, all edges. “Your brother is twenty-three.”
“Ma, I —”

“I have four minutes and a bell, so I’m not asking if you ate.” Behind her a copier thunks, and a small voice says *Mrs. Costigan* in the tone of the gravely ill. “Wait, Kyle. Gina had it at breakfast, Jackie, because Gina can’t keep a thing off a screen. By the time I got to my desk Ryan Pallante had shown his mother, and Rita had shown Father Dom’s secretary, and Father Dom’s secretary had shown *Father Dom*, who asked me at the copier whether you were eating.”
“What did you tell him?”

“That you’re a growing boy. Then his secretary showed it to me, with the sound off, in front of the copier. Everybody knows what the song’s called. I’m not going to say the name of it. It’s your brother’s birthday.”

“Danny called the house at seven, before I left. I told him there’s a video of a song and I’m not saying which. He said, *Ma, say it.* I said, *Daniel, it’s your birthday.* Then your father took the phone. He’s calling you after supper. Pick up.”
“I will.”
From the far side of the office, high and old and delighted: “*Cassidy canta!*”

“Mamma, *sit*.” The phone muffles and comes back. “She came in with me for the candles, and they gave her a chair, and she’s using it as a stage. Your father watched it in the garage on Gina’s phone, Jackie. Three times. I counted through the door. He came in the kitchen and said, *Kid can’t hold a note. Never could*, and went back out. And your brother can’t have a cake, they won’t allow it. I made the lemon one last night anyway. Your father had the first piece standing up at the counter and called it quality control.”

body.text: “And Rita Pallante printed a still of it. It’s on her refrigerator, under St. Joseph, right next to your *Yes*. She called to tell me. I thanked her for her concern.”
“She knelt Sunday and sang that Monday. That girl’s a whole liturgical year.”

body: “We bless the candles at ten,” Ma says, in the manner of a woman reading her own sentence. “The children may not light them, by order of the fire marshal, so it will be two hundred unlit candles and Kyle, who wants to know why.” A bell starts somewhere on her end and is overruled by a door. “Jackie. I watched it with the sound off. Were you *happy*?”

“Yes, Ma.” He says it before she has finished the word. Over the ridge the sun clears the oaks at last, and 412 goes from the laptop’s blue to just a room. Down on the quad the sprinklers come on in a line, one head at a time, and throw their first arcs against the light.
“Good.” A drawer slams on her end. “Then sing something else next time.”

journal.title: Ma
journal.text: Maria Costigan. St. Brigid’s school secretary. Feeds anybody who comes through the door. Cries at grace every year. Took my phone at the table and counted to eleven without looking at it once. Wrote Becca. December 6th, back from Trumbull: the November bill, four hundred and nine texts. Who is it. I told her a girl. Not Lena. Not nice — something. That’s what Dad said about her. Christmas week: took forever at the machines at Trumbull so Danny and I could talk. Stood Becca’s card at the front of the mantel. Brewed the New Orleans coffee Christmas morning. Put unlimited texting on the family plan; it was cheaper than me. Saw the photos. “Is she Catholic, at least?” When Danny laughed on the phone, she looked at me. Holy Family Sunday she took Pop in. ‘You sit, Frank.’ Showed him the machines. Goes to the seven o’clock on the last day of every year; this year I went with her. Lena called the house on the second of January, and Ma answered, and they talked for ten minutes. ‘She wants you. I don’t know why.’ Now she knows the coffee was hers. At the door she gave me the can back, empty, for the girl who called. From a gas station in Buellton I called her before I said yes on Skye’s phone. She said I was on the phone with Lena all break. I told her Lena’s still got a boyfriend, and he wrote her a song, and it was good. She didn’t say anything. Tuesday Mrs. Pallante called during dinner, and Rosie found it on the Dell before Ma got downstairs. She asked if we got married. Ma didn’t ask me what it was. She asked when I last went to confession. I said tomorrow. Then she said she’d already heard the other thing, when I said hi, so I told her: I think Skye’s the answer. Nonna heard us through the wall. ‘Go tomorrow, Jackie.’ Sunday, after the 8:00 and Trumbull: Father Dom said a prophet’s never welcome at home, and Pop said that’s for sure in the pew. She’d seen the taco picture: *she’s tiny.* Then one question — did I go up today. I said yes. She said good. Candlemas morning, from the school office between bells: my brother’s twenty-three, and Father Dom’s secretary has seen the video. She won’t say the name of the song. Pop says I can’t hold a note. She asked me if I was happy. I said yes. Sing something else next time.

journal.title: Gina
journal.text: My sister. Fifteen, a sophomore at Ursuline. Texts in lowercase like punctuation costs extra. A girl in religion class called her the class expert on visiting the imprisoned. Dad turned the radio back on. Nonna told the altar society I went to confession. Said Danny’s name back to the girl. The girl looked away first. Then laughed with Kelsey anyway. Gina wants the first part on the record. She wanted to know if the nun was real. Now they’re Facebook friends, and Lena signs her wall posts like letters. Gina found the boyfriend in about four minutes. Didn’t tell Nonna. Ashley Vrabel is going to Halloween as a prisoner. Orange jumpsuit. A tribute, she says. Lena read it once and gave me a line for her. Halloween: went as a nun, obviously. Ashley wore the jumpsuit. Gina said it — visit, not dress up as — and Kelsey laughed at Ashley for once. Ashley says she’s dead Monday. Ashley sat next to her in religion and didn’t say anything. Kelsey either. The radio says they’re firing the GM. Dad laughed, Ma says. First time since June. Tuesday she said the thing about Ashley Vrabel’s father in religion. Detention. She thought it would feel good. She heard Dad’s truck hit the can Monday night. Team Edward. Jacob is literally a dog. Monday she found Nonna at the bottom of the stairs, and called the ambulance, and went for Dad. Said sorry to Ashley. Told me in the next text. On the floor in Denver I asked her to look up a girl. She screamed. She’s sworn. ‘Not even the nun?’ Thanksgiving: met me at the door — on TV, in person. Took Danny’s call and said nothing. Printed the dock picture on Ma’s ink. Translated Nonna for Theo, mostly. Checked Facebook for me — Becca took it down. ‘You looked like you were doing a shift.’ Gave Ashley Vrabel the peace at the first candle. Still sworn. Christmas: kept it thirty days. Lifted a hand to Ashley Vrabel at the Orange Julius first, and Ashley lifted one back. Gave me the second season of *Sweetwater*, for research — and Rosie handed it to me in front of everybody. She meant upstairs. Put season two in the DVD player the day after Christmas, for research, and the whole family watched. Wrote Danny about the boat. It’s a yacht. Filmed everybody’s resolutions on Theo’s Flip. Found the baptism album before I did. “Who’s the guy?” At the door, in my ear: “Don’t let Ma find out from Facebook.” Tuesday: six thousand views; Ashley Vrabel showed the whole bus. Nonna lit a candle and won’t say for who. On my wall: FINALLY — the sister who knew first. Monday she found me on a celebrity blog before I did, and knew Danny’s jacket. A man from Mahoning County called Danny a name in the comments; she reported him, answered him, and called him one back — a Catholic one. She’s making Danny a card for Candlemas. Tuesday Ashley Vrabel showed her the picture in chem. Capitals. Wednesday, at three in the morning her time: Nonna wants a baptism name, for the rosary. Friday she was lowercase again: *mary catherine?????* Nonna said it nine times at breakfast and lit a candle for her at St. Brigid’s. My Candlemas card for Danny goes in her envelope Monday. Sunday’s Ma’s Sunday. She’s telling him in person. Tuesday, six in the morning her time, on Nonna’s computer: JACK. WHAT DID YOU DO. Then the whole homeroom. DANNYS BIRTHDAY JACK.

journal.title: Nonna
journal.text: Asked me about the girl. Laughed. Five minutes later she asked me again, the same words, like it was the first time. Ma says she’s tired. That was the nineteenth of September. Michaelmas she lit one for me and one for Danny. Saturday: ‘E la ragazza?’ Ma told her the girl has a boyfriend. ‘Peccato.’ Then, sharp: ‘E l’altra?’ Purdue Saturday. Dad said ‘Purdue’ and that was the call. Nonna got on the extension and called me Danny. Then she knew me. Then she asked about the crab girl. Sunday the 8th: ‘E la ragazza?’ Which one, I didn’t ask. She didn’t say. Monday she fell on the stairs she’d been keeping off. St. Elizabeth’s: her wrist, six stitches, a monitor for her heart. Called the paramedic handsome. Dad drove her. Home Thanksgiving morning. Cast to the elbow; a monitor on her housedress. Kept both cards — the nun’s and the other one. Made Theo her hands. Sat him in the chair. Says she’ll pray for him, starting that night. Knows it isn’t the nun. Christmas: Mémère’s still lighting her whole name — “Carmela Rinaldi. Tutto.” Asked if Danny’s coming, more than once. Set his place at the Vigil, and Ma left it. Pointed at the girl on the DVD: *l’attrice*. Theo’s cashmere is on her knees. The day after Christmas she prayed for Cassidy out loud, at the TV. *Povera.* On the Innocents she asked me to sit for the rosary, and said the intentions — for Danny, for Pop, who went in, for the nun, and for Cassidy. I told her the name’s Skye. She said Cassidy. New Year’s: lentils, a spoon each, *per i soldi*. The Befana left me coal in one of Danny’s old socks. Sugar. At the door she found me a twenty and prayed for both of us. *Tutt’e due.* Thursday night I sent Gina the name: Mary Catherine. At breakfast Nonna said *Maria Caterina* nine times, and cried the good kind, and lit a candle for her at St. Brigid’s. Candlemas she went to the school office with Ma for the candles, and heard her on the phone with me. *Cassidy canta!*

choices.text: “It was Skye’s idea. I sang the loud part.”
choices.key: On Candlemas Ma called about the video and wouldn’t say the name of the song. You told her it was Skye’s idea and you sang the loud part.
response: “That’s not the defense you think it is,” Ma says. Across the office Nonna has the last word, delighted: “*Brava!*” “Mamma, *no*.”
The bell goes, the electric kind, right through the receiver. “Eat something,” Ma says over it, and the line is gone.

choices.key: On Candlemas Ma called about the video and wouldn’t say the name of the song. You told her to tell Nonna that Cassidy’s got range.
response: Ma tells her. Word for word, across the office, to the room. Nonna’s laugh comes down the line like a kettle coming to the boil, and goes on coming.
“I’m hanging up, Jackie,” Ma says. “I have a school.”

choices.key: On Candlemas Ma called about the video and wouldn’t say the name of the song. You told her to tell Danny it was for him.
response: “I will *not*,” Ma says. Her hand goes over the receiver, and through it, muffled and scandalized, comes the room: “Mamma, he says it was *for* Danny.”
Nonna answers with something in dialect, of which Jack gets one word and Ma gets all of it. “*Mamma!*” And the line goes.

s06b.slug: TUESDAY · 2:05 PM · DELGADO HALL, THE 4TH-FLOOR LOUNGE — THE HEARING
body: The fourth-floor lounge at five past two has the flat high light that shows what the carpet has been through. The television bolted in the corner is running the morning’s hearing again, the Senate Armed Services Committee, a man in a gray suit at one end of a long table and a man in Navy blues at the other, and a crawl under them with three letters in it. The vending machine hums to itself, and on the whiteboard somebody has written HAPPY CANDLEMAS over Sunday’s raid schedule in green marker and drawn a candle with a face. Jack is passing through with half a Commons sandwich in a napkin, and he stops in the doorway.

Kevin is on the arm of the couch with the orgo text open on his knee and the cap still on his highlighter. Yusuf has the other arm and a statics problem set he is not working. On the screen an anchor with a lacquered voice is saying that Admiral Mullen, the chairman of the Joint Chiefs, told the senators that allowing gays and lesbians to serve openly “would be the right thing to do,” and that Senator McCain said he was deeply disappointed.
“Since when do you watch the news?” Jack says.

“Since it got an admiral.” Kevin doesn’t take his eyes off the screen. “I’m a sucker for a hat.” His eyes go to the napkin in Jack’s hand. “That sandwich has been out of the cooler since Sunday. I’m not saying it’s a pathogen with mayonnaise. I’m saying I’d want it looked at.”
He finds the remote on the cushion and turns the volume up one notch as the anchor reaches the admiral, and then, as she finishes, down again.
“He’s an admiral,” Kevin says, in a voice Jack can’t place. Jack takes it for rank. Kevin salutes crossing guards.
“They’ll argue about it for a year,” Yusuf says, to his problem set. “My brother says nobody in his unit asked.”
“How is Tariq?” Jack says.
“Further up the stairs every Sunday. He rates the handrails.”

Kevin mutes the set and uncaps the highlighter at last. “Clare asked me last night,” he says, “after band, over the music stands, which of you was right at Hale’s. I told her I didn’t have the information. She said that was a very Kevin answer. I think it was a compliment.”
“It was.”

“I’m logging it as one, pending review.” He lays a yellow stripe across a paragraph on the Krebs cycle, apparently at random. “Then she made me hold her music stand while she thought about it. Eleven minutes. She says that’s how she knows I’m loyal.”

body.text:
“Is today your brother’s?” Kevin asks. He saw the envelope last night, upside down on the Fishbowl table, and asked nothing then.

“Twenty-three.”
body.else: Jack checks the RAZR, finds nothing, and says it to the room. “It’s my brother’s birthday. He’s calling around four.”

body: Kevin turns from the screen for the first time since the doorway. “Is he okay?”
“He’s calling.” It is the answer Jack has.

Kevin nods and turns a page he hasn’t read. On the screen the senator is disappointed again, at greater length, and Yusuf’s pencil comes to rest on the problem set. Jack drops the sandwich in the bin by the stairs, on the strength of the medical opinion, and takes the stairs down toward Del Playa.

journal.title: Kevin Tran
journal.text: Kevin Tran. Goes to daily Mass, saves you a seat with a Bible. Has a sister, Tina, in dental school, who flossed in the womb. Lies to his mom about orgo in Vietnamese. Drives his mother’s Odyssey at sixty-five, not sixty-six. His dad has two nail-salon supply stores in San Jose and has never had a Labor Day. Brought six pairs of gloves to a beach cleanup. Mouthed every word of Joey’s first reading from the second pew. Somebody coached Joey; I can guess who. Brought tea to a wake. His Bà Nội says heaven makes the elephant and heaven makes the grass. Walked Margot down at four in the morning. Handed Lena a roll of quarters for the payphone before she asked. Halloween: All Saints, every one nobody’s heard of — scrubs, a halo and a white mask. He found Laney. Friday night a pre-med said Maine got it right. Kevin answered him and went to get water. Tuesday, the Vietnamese Martyrs: his mother reads eleven of the hundred and seventeen. Asked about the scar. Alarm Five, on the lawn: he had a question mark next to my name on his clipboard. I told Priya I was out. He erased it. Tuesday at four I woke him for Doug. A chair under the knob, then a bell. Wednesday at the Brick, at the next carrel all night: ‘You two have been defending each other for three hours. That isn’t studying.’ Sings bass. A real one. Seven years of Vietnamese choir in San Jose — his mother made him. Friday, from the Odyssey: Go home. Sleep. Tell somebody something. Back from San Jose. His mother has a girl from their parish she wants him to call. Clare. She plays the violin in the Mass band. Wednesday he brought two flats of water to the Haiti table, which nobody asked for, and stayed to hold Clare’s violin case. ‘My mother knows your mother.’ Thursday he called Clare. His mother had the number, and his grandmother was on the speaker. She said yes to Sully’s. MLK Day he brought gloves for everybody. Tuesday in the basement he read us the first reading off his BlackBerry. Clare’s going to the Walk for Life, and so is he. He asked me to come — for him. I said yes. Thursday at the window table he had a list: things to say at hour four. He’d heard about Hale’s — Laney to Margot to him — and didn’t take a side. Then he asked me what you’re supposed to feel at hour four. I told him. He wrote it down. Tuesday the admirals were on the lounge TV. He turned it up a notch, and back down. Clare asked him which of us was right at Hale’s; he told her he didn’t have the information, and she said that was a very Kevin answer. He asked if my brother’s okay.
